doc.title: Ray Vega interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 20, 2023

title: Freelancing in New York: jingle and studio dates with Chico O'Farrill
summary: After saying he moved to Vermont 15 years ago, Vega describes demanding studio and jingle work through Arturo O'Farrill, and top players like Victor Paz and Eddie Bert.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: Yeah. I mean listen, when I was in New York City, because I live in Vermont right now. I moved from Vermont to New York City when I was 46 years old. 46?
Wait a minute, you moved from New York to Vermont or the other way around? © Fillius Jazz Archive -16-

I mean from New York to Vermont. I’m in Vermont right now, I’ve been here 15 years. So I was like 46, 47 years old. Before I came up here I had to earn a living in New York City doing a wide variety of things: recording sessions, jingle dates of you don’t know what the hell it’s going to be but they don’t send you the music in advance and they don’t give you — now people have jingle dates they’ve got to call you three days — three or four days — a month in advance. “Oh I’ve got a jingle date then.” In the old days it was like you got the call the night before ‘cause the producer was just finishing maybe the rhythm tracks or something like that. Arturo O’Farrill used to get me, he was a contractor, and he used to get me on studio dates with his father. I can’t thank Arturo enough for that. But I would go in there and there would be a studio orchestra in the studio while Chico O’Farrill conducted it and we would run it, boom, in and out. We’d run it one time and at the time I think he was listening to a click track but he had the — he would see the screen where he was and he would conduct against it. And he’d go, “Okay let’s have a run through. One-two — ” and we’d run it. “Okay let’s record it. Thank you very much everybody.” And you couldn’t do that, “Oh I made a mistake.” No, no, no, no, no, no, no. You’ve got to be really, really, really prepared to go there. And I’m not saying that I was the top studio guy, hell no. But I sat there — if I walked in there and I saw Victor Paz, I would walk in and see Victor Paz on trumpet, Earl Gardner, Jimmy — what do you call that — Eddie Bert on trombone. Come on man, I’m going to go in there and start screwing around?
You’re not going to be talking either.
